title: Building spatial world models from sparse episodic memories
one_liner: Build flexible maps of the world from scattered memories instead of watching long sequences.
lead: Animals learn to navigate by stitching together random memories of places they have visited, not by watching a long movie. ESWM is a machine learning model inspired by this brain strategy—it takes disjoint fragments of experience and merges them into a coherent mental map of space, the way your brain glues together visits to different rooms into a unified building layout.

problem.h2: Why long sequences are clumsy for building maps
paras: Imagine you want to teach a robot to navigate a building. The naive way is to show it a long video: go through the lobby, up the stairs, down the hall, into the office. A typical machine learning model takes that tape, watches the whole thing frame by frame, and learns a mental picture of the space.

But that approach wastes data. If you visit the lobby three times over a month—once on Monday, once on Wednesday, once on Friday—you have three separate memories of the same place. A traditional model treating everything as one long tape cannot easily combine them. It also needs many such tapes to build a complete map. Neuroscience tells us animals do something smarter: they stitch together fragments—a Tuesday afternoon snapshot of the office, a Friday morning snapshot of the hallway, a Monday evening snapshot of the lobby—into one unified sense of place without needing hours of continuous observation.

callout.html: Build a world map from scattered single moments instead of requiring long unbroken video sequences.

steps.text: Instead of one long tape, gather separate snapshot episodes—Tuesday: I see the lobby; Thursday: I see the hall.
Train on the transitions you have seen (lobby to hall, hall to office) and predict the ones you have not.
The abstract feature space shapes itself so that nearby learned features correspond to spatially nearby places.
Ask the model to imagine a path to any location; it finds it by moving through abstract space in a way that mirrors real navigation.
Drop old memories and add new ones—the map updates instantly without relearning.

paras: ESWM changes what the model trains on: instead of requiring long sequential tapes, it takes independent snapshot-memories and learns transitions between them. This tiny shift—from 'one long tape' to 'many disjoint moments'—unlocks the whole strategy.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: spatial arrangement in abstract space
hidden.name: spatial arrangement of learned features
paras: A hidden quantity means something you cannot see directly but have to compute from observations. Here it is how the abstract features arrange themselves—the order and distances in abstract space that emerges when the model learns to represent places. In ESWM, this spatial arrangement in abstract space aligns itself to match the real geography: two learned features that are close together in abstract space correspond to two places that are close together in the real room. This is not forced by the model—it emerges because the model minimizes prediction error and discovers that mirroring real space is the best internal strategy.

The paper measures this by recording the learned feature vector for each memory (the abstract list of numbers representing each place) and comparing the distance between features in abstract space to the actual distance between places in the real environment. Strong alignment means the model's internal arrangement of features mirrors the world's layout.

heat.caption: Darker means the model measured or updated this. Highlights (borders) show the five quantities ESWM monitors.

reads.html: Spatial arrangement in abstract space is just how the abstract features organize themselves—two features close in abstract space mean two places that are similar in the real world, and this order emerges by accident as the model tries to predict transitions accurately.

The spatial arrangement alignment measures how well the learned features preserve real-world structure: the distance metric in the abstract feature space correlates strongly with actual distance in the environment, enabling zero-shot navigation.

paras: Here is the core insight: if you give a model only independent fragments, it cannot lean on temporal sequence. It must instead find a deeper pattern—the spatial rules that govern all transitions. To predict unobserved moves, the model discovers that the only efficient strategy is to place features into a space that mirrors geography. A transition from place A to place B becomes a movement through learned space that follows the same spatial logic as the real move, because that minimizes prediction error. In contrast, a model trained on long tapes can get lazy: it can memorize 'frame 42 always leads to frame 43' without learning the underlying space, because it never needs to predict a frame-to-frame jump it has never seen.

Neuroscience suggests this is how the brain works too. Animal brains store individual episodes in the hippocampus, and the brain stitches them together via spatial logic rather than temporal order. Because episodic memories can be stored and updated independently, the brain is vastly more adaptive—drop a memory, add a new one, and behavior updates instantly without rebooting the whole learning algorithm. ESWM copies this: each memory is independent, so the world model updates immediately when a new experience arrives.

stages.s: Fragment A: I see the lobby. Fragment B: I see the hall.
Extract feature vectors (abstract lists of numbers) for each place.
Predict unobserved transition: if I am in the lobby, what feature do I get in the hall?
Adjust features to make predictions accurate. Spatial arrangement emerges naturally.
A spatial map in abstract space; zero-shot navigation is free.

math.words: penalty is the squared distance between the predicted next feature and the true next feature, summed over all fragment pairs.
math.equation: loss = sum over all pairs (i, j) of squared_distance(predict_feature(fragment_i, fragment_j), true_feature_j)
symbols: a snapshot memory (e.g., the lobby visit on Monday)
another snapshot memory (e.g., the hall visit on Wednesday)
the model guesses what features it will see when it moves from fragment_i to fragment_j
the actual learned features of fragment_j
how far apart two feature vectors are (each squared to punish big errors more)

worked.title: A tiny worked example with two memories and one missing transition
lines: Memory 1 (lobby): learned features = [2, 3, 1]. Memory 2 (hall): learned features = [3, 4, 2].
Model predicts: moving from lobby to hall should give features [3.1, 3.9, 2.05].
True features of hall: [3, 4, 2]. Distance of each dimension: 0.1, 0.1, 0.05.
Squared distances: 0.01 + 0.01 + 0.0025 = 0.0225. That is the penalty for this one pair.
The model updates the features [2, 3, 1] and [3, 4, 2] slightly to lower this penalty. Repeated across all pairs, spatial arrangement aligns to space.

math.note: The key is that every fragment can be reached from any other fragment in principle—there is no fixed sequence—so the model cannot cheat with memorized temporal patterns (because it has never seen that sequence before) and must build genuine spatial arrangement that explains all transitions.

charts.title: Naive long-sequence model
charts.note: Long tapes memorize temporal patterns but fail to generalize to unseen moves or unseen destinations.

charts.title: ESWM (episodic sparse model)
charts.note: Sparse episodic training forces the model to discover spatial arrangement, enabling zero-shot reasoning.

items.html: If you train on fragments from completely different environments with no shared locations, the model cannot infer the spatial arrangement connecting them. The episodic approach works only when some experiences touch common ground.

items.b: Noisy or ambiguous place observations fail.
items.html: If a place looks different each time you visit (because of lighting, occlusion, or perceptual ambiguity), the model struggles to recognize that the same location is appearing again in different fragments, and spatial alignment breaks down.

items.b: Scalability to very large spaces is untested.
items.html: The paper shows results on modest environments. Whether the spatial arrangement remains stable and aligned as the world grows to thousands of locations is not yet demonstrated.

items.b: Done right: independent episodic updates and spatial alignment enable adaptive rapid learning.
items.html: When memories genuinely do overlap and observations are clear, ESWM achieves its promise—the model learns a flexible spatial map from fragments, updates it instantly as new memories arrive, and solves navigation and exploration without retraining.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small gridworld (a 10-by-10 room) and randomly collect 30 separate episodic memories (snapshots from random positions in the room). Each snapshot is the feature observation of that position. Train ESWM to predict the next feature when moving in cardinal directions, using only transitions you have explicitly shown. Then, without any retraining, measure two things: (1) do the learned features arrange themselves into a shape matching the grid? (2) can the model navigate successfully to a target location it has never seen in a sequence—say, 'go from bottom-left to top-right' without ever having observed that exact path during training?
demo.metric_eq: alignment_score = correlation between learned-feature distances and true grid distances; navigation_success = fraction of randomly-chosen start-goal pairs where zero-shot planning reaches the goal.
demo.closing: If ESWM truly learns from fragments, alignment should exceed 0.75 and navigation should exceed 80%, without a single additional training step after the initial 30 memories.
